speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We sought views from the public on the draft Bill in June.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: These are: R&D conducted in Singapore; registration of intellectual property (IP), including patents, trademarks and designs; acquisition and licensing of IP rights; innovation projects carried out with polytechnics, the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) or other qualified partners; and training by courses that are eligible for SkillsFuture Singapore funding and aligned with the Skills Framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This benefits businesses that have yet to turn profitable or do not have sufficient profits to maximise the benefits from the tax deductions or allowances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: In all, businesses that make full use of the scheme could enjoy tax savings amounting to nearly 70% of their investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 10, 12, 13, 14, 19, 22, 26, 34 and 54 of the Bill provide for these amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: First, we will amend our tax treatment for foreign sourced income to subject foreign sourced disposal gains to tax under specific circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This is to address international tax avoidance risks relating to non-taxation of disposal gains in the absence of real economic activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Foreign sourced disposal gains will be taxable when received in Singapore by entities of multinational enterprise groups that do not have economic substance in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Tighter rules will also apply to disposal gains arising from IP rights due to the higher mobility of such assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The policy objective of this move is not to tax capital gains in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Rather, we are making this move as part of our long-standing policy to align key areas of our tax regime with international norms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The new tax treatment is consistent with international standards, such as the rules against harmful tax practices agreed by the inclusive framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) of which Singapore is a member, as well as the European Union (EU) guidance on foreign sourced income exemption regimes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: We do not expect the new treatment to have adverse impact on our economy as our focus has always been on attracting and anchoring real economic activities in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Some businesses, however, may face increased record keeping requirements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) will work closely with the industry to minimise the compliance burden arising from this new treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clauses 6, 7 and 44 of the Bill will provide for this amendment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Second, we propose to mandate the submission of income information to IRAS by intermediaries for self-employed persons (SEPs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Since YA 2015, to simplify the tax filing process for SEPs, IRAS has been extending the pre-filling of income information scheme to SEPs and has been obtaining the income information of SEPs from intermediaries, such as commission agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The amendment will provide better clarity and certainty for intermediaries on the scope of information that may be obtained and their obligations to collect, retain and transmit the information to IRAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Beyond easing tax compliance for SEPs and facilitating tax administration, the information will also enable public agencies to better administer schemes, such as Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) by identifying the SEPS who could benefit from these schemes more easily and quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This will enable the Government to roll out future schemes in a quicker and more efficient manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: IRAS will be adopting a phased implementation approach based on the readiness of industries with SEPs, starting with commission agents from YA 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: IRAS will continue to engage the intermediaries in other industries, such as ride-hail service operators, to understand their needs and work closely with them in the onboarding process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Clause 47 of the Bill provides for these amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: Since YA 2019, IRAS has provided an option for some groups of SEPs to apply a prescribed deemed expense ratio, also known as Fixed Expense Deduction Ratio (FEDR), to calculate their net income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: This was a citizen-centric initiative: a service improvement initiative to simplify their tax-filing process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: For example, taxi and private hire car drivers can opt to use a 60% FEDR while commission agents with gross annual commission income of not more than $50,000 can opt for a 25% FEDR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: The FEDRs are reviewed regularly based on data collected to ensure that they remain relevant and reflective of the actual expenses incurred by the different groups of SEPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat) (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance)
text: To provide greater convenience to another group of SEPs, we propose to extend the FEDR option to self-employed delivery workers who are earning gross annual delivery income of up to $50,000.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad this year is no different, as we seek to make our tax system fairer, easier to use and an important lever to boost our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just like the last few years, this Bill implements the tax changes announced by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance during the Budget Statement in February 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One significant change is to the Working Mother's Child Relief (WMCR), which allows working mothers to enjoy deductions to their taxable income for each additional child they have.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From my conversations with young couples, I understand that some are frustrated that this move penalises higher-income mothers as they would enjoy less tax benefits than before.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even though I clarify that they will continue to enjoy the percentage tax deductions for any child born before 1 January 2024, the fact remains that mothers earning more than $4,500 per month will get less benefit than before for any future child.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the aim is "to encourage couples in all income groups to have children", as Deputy Prime Minister explained in his Budget round-up speech, did the Ministry consider retaining the percentage deductions while adding fixed dollar floors to the deductible income?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would allow lower-income mothers to gain more without being at the expense of higher-income mothers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On a related note, I notice that the Bill also removes the deduction allowed to a woman in relation to the levy she or her husband pays for a domestic helper.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is the underlying basis for such a deduction no longer relevant today?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   The Bill also introduces a new provision for IRAS to require prescribed persons to collect, retain and submit income information for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the list of prescribed persons has not been announced yet, I expect that it will include platforms and ride-hailing companies who would be able to process such information for the delivery riders and private-hire drivers that they work with.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, what other types of intermediaries does the Ministry expect to prescribe in subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also understand that a phased implementation approach will be adopted.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Ministry share how it expects to do this?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will this come into effect for next year's income tax filing for YA 2023?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am a strong advocate of the use of data and technology to push and deliver Government support schemes to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, there may be good reasons why SEPs do not want their income data to be collected and retained by other persons, including the operators of the platforms which they might be providing their services on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will it be compulsory for SEPs to participate once IRAS issues a notice to the third-party intermediary to collect, retain or provide income data, or will SEPs be able to opt in or opt out?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, finally, I am supportive of the move to enhance the tax incentives for qualifying expenditure on R&D.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the World Economic Forum Global Risks Report 2023 ranked the cost-of-living crisis as the top ranked global risk by severity over the next two years, given stubborn inflationary pressures, food supply and energy supply concerns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Domestically, while one can argue that inflation rates have been trending down in recent months, where the latest data for August 2023 has Consumer Price Index-All Items inflation easing to 4% year-on-year in August from 4.1% in July, it is important to note that this is still significantly higher than what we have been used to in Singapore, when inflation rates have averaged a mere 1% to 2% in the last four decades.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the second order effects on inflation from increases in basic utilities, transportation and fresh shocks to global energy and food commodity prices have yet to be fully seen on consumer prices, which could result in persistent price pressures in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving from the individual Singaporean's point of view to that of the Government's position, now that we are close to the halfway mark in terms of the financial year, it is also timely to reevaluate the Government's current fiscal position against what was initially projected as per Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a quick recap, I shared in my Budget debate speech that the Government's fiscal position turned out to be better than expected in the last two financial years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budget 2023, the Government expects operating revenues to increase by $6.4 billion to a record high of $96.7 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, the increase in revenues that was expected for the whole of FY2023 was already surpassed at the five-month mark.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Meanwhile, expenditures in the first quarter of FY2023 have been stable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we set the cost-of-living crisis, which is threatening the living standards of many Singaporeans, against what will likely be a better-than-expected fiscal position for the Government in yet another year of record high collections of corporate income tax, personal income tax and even GST, I find it difficult not to feel a strong sense of injustice and imbalance here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This leads me to my next point about the hike in GST rate from 8% to 9%, which is all set to go ahead from 1 January 2024 despite the circumstances I have described.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the conclusion of the Budget Debate, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shared that, "We have to proceed with the second step of the increase in GST in 2024 as planned.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deferring this will only store up more problems for the future and will leave us with less resources to take care of our growing number of seniors." Even if I am personally resigned to the fact that no matter what my objections to the GST rate increase are and that the Government is adamant that the alternatives that the Workers' Party has put forth will not be accepted, could we not, at the very least, defer the planned increase in GST in 2024?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even with a one percentage point increase in the GST thus far, the Government expects GST revenues in FY2023 to be $2.9 billion higher than FY2022 – close to what the full GST hike was supposed to bring in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we compare FY2023 GST revenues against that in FY2021, then GST revenues would be $4.7 billion higher.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With Government revenues already better than initially projected at the five-month mark, is it that difficult to delay the second step of the GST increase and will this delay result in us storing up more problems for the future and leave us with less resources to take care of our growing number of seniors, as shared by Deputy Prime Minister Wong in the Budget 2023 round-up speech?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I leave Singaporeans to draw their own conclusions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared in my Budget debate speech earlier this year, while there could be a group of lower-income working mothers who would benefit marginally from this change, the majority of would-be working mothers will be worse off with the change in methodology.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Based on my estimates of working mothers' income within married couples in resident households, roughly 20% of mothers will benefit from the WMCR changes while the remaining 80% of mothers will either be unaffected or worse off.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I wonder if WMCR truly seeks to reward families with children and encourage married women to remain in the workforce after having children, or does it have the unintended opposite effect?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To further support lower-income working mothers, if the tax rebates granted exceed the tax payable, tax credits can be paid out in cash to ensure the reliefs are not lost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, unwed single mothers are ineligible for this relief.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But what about the next 15 years' of tax assessments for the working mother?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would she be better off or worse off with the WMCR change?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps a reversion of WMCR to what it previously was could be considered as part of the "A Singapore Made for Families 2025" plan, which is supposed to affirm our whole-of-society effort to create a family-friendly Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude in Mandarin, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although I am aware that the Government announced a one-off assistance package last month, with prices of many daily necessities soaring recently and the second-order effect on inflation from global energy and food prices not yet fully reflected in local prices, the cost-of-living pressures faced by Singaporeans may continue for some time, if not, increase.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The proposed amendments to the Income Tax Act put into effect some key measures to drive incentives to bolster our economy and to support Singaporeans, as announced in Budget 2023.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will speak today on two changes that are relevant to parties at the opposite ends of the economic spectrum: firstly, for the very rich, the amendments related to the Philanthropy Tax Incentive Scheme (PTIS) for family offices; and, secondly, the amendments related to mandating the submission of income information by intermediaries for SEPs, a segment of our population with a significant share of lower-income workers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These tax incentives complement other changes announced at Budget 2023, including allowing family offices to meet the minimum local spending requirement via charitable donations and grants to blended finance structures as well as the inclusion of climate-related investments and blended finance structures for the purposes of the Capital Deployment Requirement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Taken together, it is a really exciting bet on the role of philanthropic capital linked to family offices in catalysing much needed investment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The increasingly global nature of many of the challenges facing the world – from food and health security to education gaps and climate change – requires increasingly global responses and resources.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By absorbing risks and lowering costs, philanthropic capital can play a key role alongside development and public finance to mobilise the needed private capital, for example, in the form of blended finance structures.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To me, the design of PTIS is well thought through.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It clearly reflects the Government's intent to build Singapore's philanthropic ecosystem linked to family offices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The changes could result in a higher proportion of higher quality family offices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Tax incentives for cross-border philanthropy are not so common globally, but Singapore is not unique in the region in encouraging family offices to deploy capital towards philanthropic causes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Hong Kong has also recently introduced tax concessions for family-owned investment holding vehicles (FIHVs) and provided that approved charities in Hong Kong may hold up to 25% beneficial interest in such FIHVs, in order to encourage FIHVs to invest in charitable assets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But mobilisation of capital is only part of the story.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For greater impact, collective action is needed of players across the finance and investment ecosystems to get more creative, trying new approaches for accelerating investments in order to drive meaningful innovation and actions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It requires new partnerships, new skills, new ways of thinking, including systems thinking and systems innovation, to achieve the scale of change the world needs right now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Against this context, I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The amendments provide for the Minister or authorised body to approve a person or persons as approved donors and recipients.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How long does it take for a family office, already approved under section 13O or section 13U or new to Singapore to be approved as a donor, or for a local charity or intermediary to be approved as a qualifying local intermediary?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) ensure that the approval processes do not discourage new and smaller philanthropic entities, but with perhaps key strengths and capabilities to apply?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What level of oversight will there be on the actual use of the philanthropic contributions?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will MAS approach and manage the administrative and compliance requirements of philanthropic entities operating abroad, and often be in partnership with local entities and local laws?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government work with the ecosystem to build the capabilities and skills of the players in the philanthropy ecosystem domestically, but also internationally through partnerships with organisations, perhaps further down the learning curve to drive greater impact?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Is there room to consider for some portion of the contributions to be made directly to a very select list of international organisations and yet qualify for the tax incentives?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In July, I had asked a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on the economic contribution of single family offices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But let us never forget that finance has been, can be and must be a force for good.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Philanthropies can and must get creative to go beyond channelling aid to unlocking and catalysing investment into the biggest challenges of our time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Family offices can contribute to this new philanthropy ecosystem and be a force for good and I support PTIS.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would now like to shift to the amendments related to submission of income of SEPs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have to admit that this news has led to some level of consternation on the ground, but it is the right thing to do, for those who earn an income beyond a reasonable threshold to accurately report their income, whatever their level of income.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is how we do right by one another, how everyone takes responsibility and how we keep being a team.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to have faith in the system, that if we need help, we will get it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is equally the Government's responsibility to accurately assess the income tax of each hardworking Singaporean worker, and to be proactive and responsive when the data tells us that something has changed in the worker's situation and to extend support when needed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Because we know full well the vulnerabilities of being self-employed – how sickness and injury mean zero income for the day or, worse, months, like for my resident who has met with an accident recently.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, this proposed change, by increasing transparency for tax assessment, must also make it easier, more automatic, for schemes that are designed to support Singaporean SEPs to be administered and minimise onerous submission of information each time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, I continue to hear feedback on the ground from some drivers that they are taking home less and, in some cases, significantly less.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And could the submission of income information automatically allow for more timely and accurate assessment of the sufficiency of the FEDR by assessing patterns and trends across the population for each category of SEPs?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Two, how can the possession of timely income information for SEPs facilitate the design and administration of Government schemes to support SEPs, in particular to address the vulnerabilities of SEPs?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The tax system, when well-designed and well-understood, strengthens the relationship and the accountability between the Government and the people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Government has strived over the years to build a comprehensive, fair and sustainable tax system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Bill before us is an omnibus one that includes a slate of proposed amendments associated with the 2023 Budget, along with almost as many that improve tax administration and align policy objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has already expressed its reservations with respect to several components of this year's Budget, especially the continued insistence on an increase in the GST, along with our concerns over the design of WMCR, which we continue to hew to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have also expressed our support for other elements that we believe are net positives, including tax incentives for R&D and an increase in the Central Provident Fund (CPF) monthly ceiling, that will go toward improving the business environment while also supporting workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In light of this, I will focus my remarks, first, on thoughts related to non-Budget measures proposed in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will then go on to address an issue within the spirit of the Bill – the use and timing of taxes for fulfilling economic objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will, first, offer an assessment of our current economic situation before explaining why I believe that rebating taxes in full is not only a responsible policy choice, but the only right thing to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not necessarily a negative development, especially since a segment of delivery workers may be among the lower-income segments of our society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I wonder if these FEDRs will require these workers to claim the exemptions themselves, or if any such claims will be automatically filed by their companies when they report their employee earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this approach could well be unusual, but if certain delivery riders are less tech- as well as tax-savvy, they may be unfamiliar with the intricacies of claims for tax exemptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I also say this because, at least based on clause 44 of the Bill, the entire point of the amendments related to SEPs is to simplify the tax filing process, and a complicated claims procedure would surely go against that purported aim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a welcome move because, as the Ministry has itself acknowledged, the relevance of purchased life annuity has been diminished and it makes eminent sense to tie returns to a more credible and robust measure, such as SORA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) recognises the importance of ensuring that only credible interest rates are used as our benchmarks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But yet, this reminds me of other increasingly obsolete rates, those for short-term fixed deposits as well as saving accounts, for which CPF Ordinary Account interest rates are derived.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the local context, the problem with these rates is that they have, similarly, become increasingly removed from the rates that banks genuinely offer to their customers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even the SORA itself has transacted at between 3.6% and 4% over the past month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I agree with the thrust of the measures proposed, I would also like to put it to this House that the long-term considerations that are the preoccupation of much of the Bill should also take into account shorter-term matters that concern the regular folk in our country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, coffee shop chatter often likes to speak about how this Government gives out chicken wings, only to take back a whole chicken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While pithy, I do not particularly enjoy this characterisation because I understand that part of the essential functions of Government include redistribution and public good provision, for which raising taxes is ultimately part and parcel of meeting expenditure needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, in a sense, the Government is always in the business of giving away as well as taking back chickens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But where the aphorism rings true is when there is a perceived imbalance between what taxpayers fork out and what they believe they are getting back in benefits and entitlements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, our system remains largely progressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, those in the lowest income undoubtedly get more than what they put into the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is the case in virtually every high-income country in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It would be an exceedingly low bar to benchmark our expectations of Government as one that does not engage in regressive taxation on net.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, we should ask ourselves if the Government is doing enough to support the least fortunate in our midst or if it can do more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the squeezed middle-class is receiving crucial support, especially when costs of living are rising at a rapid clip and if Singaporean households are feeling increasingly squeezed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If society can ask those who have been the luckiest in the economic sweepstakes to give back a little bit more to the system that they have benefitted so much from.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, it is not so much about chickens or chicken wings, it is about whether the people are getting the support today at a time when they need it or if they are being asked to sacrifice more at a time when finances at home are already increasingly tight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, is it a good time then to be asking for chickens or should the Government be giving out more chickens at this time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although we managed to avoid a recession thus far, Singapore's economy remains undeniably fragile.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Further headwinds are to be expected, given the downturn in the global electronics cycle, on which our manufacturing sector remains heavily dependent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The general weakness in growth is acknowledged by both the Government and private sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The median GDP forecast among respondents to the Survey of Professional Forecasters was just 1% in September, down from 1.4% in June.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Concomitantly, the labour market also appears to be cooling, with labour demand falling for the fifth consecutive quarter, along with a dip in job vacancies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Prices are still rising faster than is comfortable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Looking below the hood, inflation in key survival sectors – food, accommodation and transport – are even higher, and the recent inflation picture has been a little flattered by collapsing energy prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the recent and impending price hikes on a range of things, such as Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC), electricity and gas tariffs, postage and public transport, will likely apply upward pressure on inflation, going forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may yet avoid a recession but are heavily dependent on international economic conditions which are weak in both China and Europe, two key engines for global growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In spite of this softness in the real economy, inflation, while down from the peaks of last year, cannot yet be regarded as tamed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, it is hard to fathom why we would want the fiscal impulse from the Government to be a further drag on the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Estimates are that fiscal revenues rose by 0.7% of GDP as a result of the GST hike alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is even before the anticipated increase by another percentage point for GST come January next year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is in this context that I had previously stressed the importance of rebating back, as much as possible, any surpluses the Government will earn arising from the simple fact that tax revenues – much of which are levied in percentage terms – would almost certainly rise in absolute terms due to inflation alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At that time, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated unequivocally, in a response to our claim that a surplus would likely emerge, that, and I quote, "I wish that were so, but unfortunately, we do not have any surplus".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, part of this would have been due from unspent expenditures accrued from careful spending as well as additional receipts due to unexpectedly vigorous economic activity, especially in the real estate sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But undoubtedly, a non-trivial part of this is also the simple fact that tax receipts are elevated because inflation has become elevated, resulting in greater receipts in nominal terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government, in tandem with announcements over the hikes to utilities, also indicated that there will be a Cost-of-Living Package to help offset the increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this method of effecting lump-sum transfers, instead of rolling out subsidies, is an approach that would be recommended by most economists, and it is my preferred approach as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, some murmurings on the ground have griped about how these packages are only one-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And that is true, although this is based on a presumption that wages will eventually catch up, thereby making most wage-earning households whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So far, however, wages have barely kept up – gross salaries grew, in real terms, by only 0.4% last year, and in terms of basic wages, they shrank a full percentage point.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And so, I would urge the Government to stand ready with continued support, should the erosion of take-home salaries persist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, a pass-through of any tax windfall should not be viewed as Government largesse, but as arising from the simple arithmetic of how inflation simply bumps up the nominal price of everything, including tax revenues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, rebating surpluses is not about generosity at all, but simply a moral imperative that the Government not profit from rising prices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Income Tax (Amendment) Bill evokes a range of emotions in workers and firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Workers and firms appreciate that the Bill provides certainty on the "what".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, ensuring data is simple to interpret, yet accurate and complete.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This includes delivery workers using online matching platforms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is to be based on a prescribed percentage of annual gross income from freelance delivery work and is subject to an income cap.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: At present, self-employed commission agents, taxi drivers and private hire car drivers benefit from similar "FEDR" arrangements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Joseph Goh, a private-hire car driver of close to eight years, appreciates that the FEDR frees him from needing to derive the expense figure for his yearly tax filing.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: But he worries that a predetermined FEDR could become outdated and over-simplified.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Other private-hire car drivers and taxi drivers share his worry.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Self-employed delivery workers now share this worry too.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They ask: does the data behind the FEDR reflect the reality of climbing operating costs, such as higher fuel prices and pricier vehicle leases?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Has the data considered operational complexities such as how different elements impact platform work?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Or the multi-fold impact of GST on drivers and riders' incomes?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, Mr Goh has little choice but to absorb the GST that is imposed on his vehicle rental, commissions payable, servicing fees, fuel costs and so on.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These platform workers therefore seek assurance from the Government that the FEDRs are determined using accurate and complete data and are reviewed periodically.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to my second point: adopting pro-worker perspectives to data collection.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Another new section – 68A of the principal Act – grants the Government power to require any person, whom I shall refer to as X, who belongs to a prescribed class of persons to comply with a notice that may require X to collect and retain identification and income and expenses information of any person, whom I shall name as Y, who entered into an agreement or arrangement of a specific description with X for carrying on any trade, business, vocation or profession for which Y derives chargeable income.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Examples of X may include commission-paying agencies and taxi or platform operators.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Section 68A makes certain that the Government would have visibility of platform workers' income and expense information if the Government so decides.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This visibility makes platform workers wonder how such information would be used and how its use would be safeguarded.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They also wonder if the Government's heightened awareness of platform workers' income challenges would translate to policy-makers becoming more proactive in engaging the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and its representative affiliated associations on more support for platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: After all, "with great power comes great responsibility" goes the saying familiar to most Spiderman fans.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Platform workers thus seek to be assured that the FEDRs would be accurate, complete and indicative of the operating cost challenges of taxi drivers, private-hire car drivers and delivery workers, for their respective vocations and as platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This concern has been raised by Labour Movement Members of Parliament at various Parliament Sittings since Year 2020, if I recall.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, could the Minister share how the Government intends to ensure continual relevance of the FEDRs?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, devising pro-company approaches to encourage firm-based innovation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also makes certain economic support for Singapore businesses desiring to innovate.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By tapping on EIS to innovate, small firms can aspire to outcompete larger firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Firms with more modest ambitions, too, can tap on the EIS to embark on process innovation, a journey that can also inspire in their workforce the courage to experiment.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Whether firms seek to innovate for incremental gain or transformative technology, smaller firms generally find it challenging to set aside capital for innovation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Scarred by the pandemic, small firms tend to prioritise profitability and accumulation of reserves over risk and vague promises of success.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Wanting to enhance its existing product to cater to a new market, a small firm, Firm X, decided to partner a local polytechnic on an innovation project.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Firm X was quick to apply to Enterprise Singapore for project funding under the EIS.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It was then that Firm X realised that it could be out of a substantial amount of cash for up to a year if it proceeded.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This was because Firm X had to pay the polytechnic upfront before it could commence the project.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, it could only submit the claims for reimbursement after the completion of the project.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Firm X was also informed that it might only receive the reimbursements three to six months after claim submissions.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To protect its cash position, Firm X decided to reduce its cash outlay and in turn the project scope.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While this slowed Firm X's progress, its founders felt that conserving cash would put Firm X on surer footing to navigate the economic uncertainty.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: While these are praiseworthy initiatives, cash-tight firms like Firm X might still hesitate from setting aside adequate budget for innovation-related spending.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: But this hesitation might waver if subsidies were given upfront.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A pro-company approach could thus involve mirroring the existing arrangement for course fee subsidy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Approved institutions partnering these EIS-supported firms could offset the subsidy amounts from this block budget.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, under this arrangement, EIS-supported firms would only have to pay a fraction of the project cost.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A pro-company approach could lower firms' barriers to innovation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These firms' workforce would benefit from exposure to innovation activities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation-led growth could open doors for workers to build skills in new areas and to embark on new prospects.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, firms might want to enter the metaverse.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Local creative freelancers with the right skillsets could create metaverse relevant digital assets for these firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Government consider working with umbrella organisations, such as NTUC's Visual, Audio, Creative Content Professionals Association, to provide financial support to freelancers when they train for new opportunities?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like small firms, such support would go a long way to ease the financial burden on freelancers when they trade-off present gigs to invest in future skills.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, platform workers need assurance that data used to determine the FEDRs is simple to interpret yet accurate and complete.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, platform workers want to know how their information would be used and safeguarded if platforms are to release it to the Government, and whether the Government, being better informed, would engage representative organisations like the NTUC to introduce more support for platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, small firms can be encouraged to innovate if innovation projects were co-paid upfront.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Government could also support freelancers who want to train for future-oriented work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These freelancers could cater to the new needs of innovating firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding these three points which I hope the Minister could consider, I thank the Minister for this comprehensive and progressive Bill.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The EIS, with its increased tax deductions and allowances, is poised to have a significant impact on business innovation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It encourages businesses to invest in R&D and IP registration, which can lead to the development of new products, services and technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The EIS can give Singapore businesses a competitive advantage on the global stage by providing enhanced tax allowances.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is especially true in today's highly competitive and rapidly changing business environment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Introducing tax breaks for qualifying innovation projects with selected partner institutions is a progressive step.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It fosters knowledge exchange and potentially game-changing innovations by encouraging collaboration between businesses and educational or research institutions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It broadens participation, while also enhancing its developmental and translational potential.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It provides flexibility and immediate financial relief, which can be beneficial to startups and small businesses with limited cash flow.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To make it easier for businesses to navigate the scheme and to take full advantage of the incentives, can the Minister provide more information and specific guidelines on eligibility criteria, application processes and documentation requirements?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In terms of awareness and outreach, many businesses may be unaware of the scheme's benefits, a well-crafted and proactive outreach can increase participation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, how will the MOF conduct awareness campaigns and workshops to educate businesses about EIS?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Long-term commitment to such incentives can provide businesses with the stability and assurance needed for sustained innovation efforts.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is prudent to establish a balanced framework of monitoring and evaluation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Regular evaluation can aid in assessing the effectiveness of incentives and making necessary changes or improvements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Maintaining transparency in the allocation of incentives and an accountability system in the use of funds will protect the scheme's integrity and long-term viability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As such, what are the mechanisms established when tracking the performance and impact of EIS over time?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To summarise, the EIS has the potential to stimulate Singapore's innovation and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To maximise its impact, it is critical to provide clarity, raise awareness and continuously evaluate its effectiveness while keeping long-term commitment and inclusivity in mind.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The second part is on the philanthropy tax.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The PTIS for Family Offices demonstrates Singapore's commitment to philanthropy on a local and global scale.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It represents a bold step forward in harnessing wealth and generosity for the greater good.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: First and foremost, this programme is intended to increase the impact of philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We hope to channel significant resources towards causes that truly matter.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: By incentivising family offices to establish their giving operations in Singapore, this initiative has the potential to attract both wealth and talent to our shores.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When family offices choose Singapore as their philanthropic hub, it enriches both our financial and philanthropic sectors, fostering an environment in which both innovation and giving thrive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This reinforces our vision of Singapore as a global philanthropic hub.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, there are considerations and suggestions to consider.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As with any significant policy change, transparency and accountability are of the utmost importance.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must also put in place robust monitoring mechanisms to ensure that the scheme achieves its goals and impact.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This scheme will rely heavily on public reporting and impact assessments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Encouraging family offices to report their philanthropic activities can help to build trust and confidence in the scheme's effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Collaboration through family offices, local intermediaries and charitable organisations should be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We can maximise the positive impact of philanthropic donations and make a significant difference in our communities by working together.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We should encourage our family offices to support charitable organisations in Singapore and promote local philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our local community deserves our help and generosity as well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The PTIS for family offices is an exciting and innovative initiative.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It has the potential to affect positive change on a global scale while enhancing our own philanthropic ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Let us embark on this journey to become a regional, if not global, philanthropy hub with a sense of purpose and transparency, dedicated to making the world a better place for all.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These changes seek to align our tax rules with that set out in the EU Code of Conduct Group (COCG) guidance.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite a dramatic change in Singapore's income tax landscape and I would like to seek the following clarifications from the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, what are the reasons for enacting section 10L at this time?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It has been announced that more comprehensive international tax-related amendments concerning Pillar 2 of the BEPS initiative will only be implemented from 2025.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister be able to contexualise Singapore's wider roadmap towards compliance with these new international tax norms?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification has to do with the interpretation of the new section 10L.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I note that in the response to the public consultation on the Bill, the MOF has indicated that the IRAS will provide further guidance on the concept of "economic substance" through an e-tax guide to be issued.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is expected to provide more detailed examples for certain specific sectors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are some aspects of section 10L which can be clarified further and, in particular, those relating to the definition of an "excluded entity" at section 10L(16).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Reference is made here to a pure equity-holding entity having "adequate human resources and premises in Singapore".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is not clear whether this assessment will be an objective test adopted by the authorities or a subjective one, which will be based on what the taxpayer fairly represents in the context of its operations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are also doubts as to how the term "direct and effective control" will be interpreted.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This was a requirement added only after the public consultation process.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some aspects of it can be explained further.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, it is not clear how it will be applied in the context of a fund entity which has outsourced discretionary management to a fund manager in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Professional commentators have further noted that it would be useful to set up a system of expedited advance rulings on the determination of "economic substance" in order to assist taxpayers and it is not immediately apparent from the legislation if such a system will be made available.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, it is also unclear as to how section 10L will interact with the present administrative concessions on the operation of section 10(25) and the deemed remittance of foreign-sourced income.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One particular example is the present concessionary treatment for foreign businesses which are not operating in or from Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They are able to remit their foreign income to Singapore without being taxed on such income.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am given to understand that this concession is in place to begin with to encourage the use of Singapore's banking systems and facilities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To summarise, there are some aspects of section 10L which remain unclear.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore like to ask if the Senior Minister of State can clarify the extent to which more detailed guidance and examples will be provided in order to assist taxpayers in their interpretation of this new law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that tax practitioners have written to the authorities to seek clarifications on these technical points and more, and I hope that more detailed guidance will follow.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While I fully agree that we should indicate our strong commitment to evolving international tax norms, we should balance this commitment with the need to provide clarity to businesses that wish to engage in or with Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The PTIS is being introduced in order to strengthen Singapore's position as a regional philanthropy hub.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is also put in place to encourage family offices to anchor their giving operations in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On this provision, I have two clarifications for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State be able to clarify what is intended by this provision and what kinds of conditions are envisioned?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Subsection (10) provides for a clawback of the tax deduction granted if fund managers of incentivised funds fail to adhere to conditions which are imposed later in time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: According to the MAS website, the PTIS will also require that qualifying Single Family Offices (SFOs) should increase their headcounts, and this includes the hiring of philanthropy professionals.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It has also been announced that donations should be made through certain local qualifying intermediaries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at these measures in totality, it appears that there is a push towards helping local charities to develop their expertise in supporting overseas charitable giving and towards growing philanthropic capabilities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That being said, it is also clear that the PTIS is primarily intended to allow family offices to obtain tax advantages in respect of their overseas giving.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What then could result is a "race" for donations, whether perceived or real, with local charities feeling as though they have a new source of competition for funding.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Charities in Singapore do not always have an easy time with fundraising.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: From the National Arts Council's Arts Philanthropy Corporate Giving Research findings, which surveyed 470 respondents last year, companies agreed that corporate giving to the arts is important to build a vibrant community and a connected society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless of this awareness, businesses were still not motivated to give to the arts sector, possibly because such benefits were not deemed to be as direct from a business perspective.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The research report concludes that more can be done to better articulate how a vibrant community underpinned by the arts can be good for businesses.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The statistics in Singapore seem to bear this out.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: DECK is an arts centre for photography and registered IPC in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is presently fundraising to build a permanent art centre for photography and amongst the visual art community, it is well known as being a big supporter of both emerging and established artistic talent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Gwen Lee, who is the co-founder and director of DECK, once told me that fundraising for her charity is like carrying the weight of the Himalayas on her shoulders all the time.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is little respite and there is constant worry about how staff will be paid and how they will meet their compliance obligations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: DECK is just one example, of course, from the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a similar concern faced by many local charities which often operate with lean teams and on stretched budgets.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This diversity is important because an over-reliance on Government funding and subsidies in the arts is neither sustainable in the long term, nor is it desirable in terms of the substance and quality of artistic production.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Particularly, in the context of arts charities, this could be useful in providing new perspectives on art making within our local creative community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that when administering the PTIS, local charitable entities are brought to the attention of approved donors as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The rising tide of foreign philanthropy in Singapore should result in all charitable boats being lifted to greater heights.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This proposal is significant as it marks a key and fundamental shift in Singapore's longstanding policy of not taxing gains of a capital nature.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This change is largely driven by a multilateral tax policy-making environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, Singapore may be monitored by the EU, with potential repercussions for Singapore's reputation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This proposed change by MOF may lead companies to reconsider the best place to receive such gains.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How many multinational enterprises (MNEs) will be affected by this amendment in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will this affect our global appeal due to the uncertainty over the impact on investment vehicles?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will MNEs incur taxes if the foreign assets are sold as part of an internal restructuring?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is the gain derived from subtracting the net book value from the open market value?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the sale of the foreign asset is to a related Singapore company, would the Ministry consider making an exception to accept the use of net book value as sale value for internal restructuring purposes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another potential area of ambiguity concerns investment entities, such as special purpose vehicles set up by investment funds and family offices.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does a special purpose vehicle which have not applied for the fund tax incentive scheme need to prove that it is a pure equity-holding entity in order to qualify for exclusion?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would now like to comment on MOF's proposal to require intermediaries, such as real estate and insurance companies, to submit the income data of SEPs directly to IRAS.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support this as it will facilitate the income tax assessment of these SEPs, as well as the administration of schemes that cover SEPs, such as the WIS and various support grants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When will this be extended to other intermediaries, such as parcel deliverers and taxi operators?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a good proposal as it removes the hassle of SEPs having to input their tax submission and ensures accuracy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SEPs will have a lighter administrative workload and fewer concerns about wrong declarations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, will the PTIS be applicable for philanthropic funds that finances sustainable projects located overseas like the retirement of coal fired power plants?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can philanthropic funds which invest in and help Singaporean small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to decarbonise qualify for this scheme too?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How about philanthropic funds which invest in the mitigation of climate change globally, in other words, the beneficiaries are located overseas?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has to strengthen the ecosystem of compassion, capital and expertise to tackle the crisis of global warming and loss of biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The abovementioned proposed changes can encourage funds to pay more attention to the social causes that require investment, impact and compassion.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   At a time when business costs are high, disbursing resources to pursue innovation is unlikely to be top of mind for most business owners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the current macroeconomic climate presents the best timing to invest in innovation so as to offset some costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But any Government scheme is only as good as its utilisation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope Government can work with the SME centres, business associations, business consultants and the Centres of Innovation to promote EIS to the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can EIS be used to fund the education and upskilling of staff which are foundational to developing an innovative mindset and maximising the value technology can bring to their businesses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It is now my pleasure to call on Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant for his maiden speech in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, the EIS is poised to be a game changer for our economy as these deductions are very good for businesses, especially SMEs and important for workers who aspire to excel, improve themselves and keep themselves abreast with the need for improved skills in an ever-changing global environment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of the EIS is a holistic approach to anchor high value-creation activities in Singapore by providing companies with added incentives to undertake R&D activities in Singapore, acquire IP rights and upskill and transform the workforce.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These deductions are designed to foster the growth of businesses that operate in the digital sphere, which is increasingly becoming the mainstay of trade and commerce.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses can now deduct startup expenses related to business advisory, account creation, content creation, product listing and placement.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The next area I would like to discuss is maintaining overseas offices and the deductions that are available for that.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As our economy becomes increasingly interconnected globally, maintaining overseas trade offices is crucial for businesses to expand their international reach.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As we adapt to the digital age and the ever-expanding global marketplace, we recognise the need to support businesses that operate internationally and engage in electronic commerce.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The deduction for expenses related to overseas trade offices will encourage businesses to establish and sustain these offices, fostering trade relationships and enhancing our country's global presence.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In a rapidly evolving global landscape, innovation is key to success for businesses and nations.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Economic progress enhances competitiveness and improves our standard of living.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Introducing this new tax deduction for qualifying expenditure incurred in pursuing innovation projects is a visionary good policy that aligns with our nation's commitment to innovation and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: More SMEs should tap on the EIS for innovation, IP and training expenses in order to access digital and green economy opportunities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Well, the world is changing and we in Singapore have to change with it.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The spirit of this change is to align our tax practices with the EU COCG guidance, which aims to mitigate international tax avoidance risks.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Other jurisdictions, such as Hong Kong, are implementing similar rules to avoid being on the COCG's blacklist.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Previously, the cornerstone of Singapore's tax system was that it does not tax capital gains.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This change, however, introduces capital gains tax into the Singapore system and perhaps represents a fundamental change to our tax system.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: A potential sort of impact of this change is that some corporates, fund management companies and family offices, may consider relocating their holding companies to other global jurisdictions, such as Dubai or the United Kingdom, resulting in a loss of opportunities and jobs within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, one very positive outcome of this tax Bill could be that these entities may instead choose to increase their economic substance in Singapore by expanding their operations and business so that they are exempt from this new tax.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Needless to say, such increased business activity can only help our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In the larger scheme of things, the Government needs to continue to reiterate its pro-investment and pro-business stance by clearly communicating the rationale for the shift and its continued commitment to providing a stable and trusted regime for both individuals and companies with investment and holding structures.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The second area is on submitting income information for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative aims to streamline income tax assessment for SEPs and facilitate the administration of schemes, such as the WIS.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I have the following suggestions to make which perhaps the Government can explore in the implementation of this initiative.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Would the income tax department consider exploring the possibility of combining this roll-out with upcoming changes with regards SEPs serving as platform workers and who may require a structured and standardised way to achieve financial inclusion?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Can the platforms enabling employment for SEPs, be classified as intermediaries and be provided with financial support to establish this new infrastructure for regulatory reporting?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We have often heard from our SMEs in a variety of sectors, that it is quite a challenge for them to keep pace and track the changes made to the tax system after each Budget.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would encourage MOF to have regular roadshows post-Budget as well as distribute focused, short information brochures through various digital channels throughout the financial year.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Such consistent, focused messages are very useful for our smaller businesses to easily comprehend and then take necessary action to make sure that they do not lose out on the benefits that they could accrue and gain from the changes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Key amendments, such as tax gains from the sale of foreign assets that are received in Singapore by businesses without economic substance in Singapore and mandating the submission of income information by intermediaries by SEPs better improve tax administration and policy objectives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The PTIS for family offices strengthens Singapore's position as a regional philanthropy hub and encourages family offices to anchor their operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And the EIS enhances the already available tax incentives and aims to encourage more businesses to engage in R&D, innovation and capability development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was described that 2022 was a year of "brutal inflation" worldwide where global inflation was around 9% and inflation reached historic levels in many advanced economies, such as the United States and Germany.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To battle this inflation, MAS had tightened our monetary policy five times since October 2021.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Amidst higher prices, including higher conservancy prices, higher water prices and higher transport prices, the additional $1.1 billion Cost-of-Living Support Package for households aims to offset these price increases with the additional S&CC rebate, U-Save rebate and Public Transport Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to that, all Singaporean households receive $200 of Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers and 2.5 million eligible adult Singaporeans will receive up to $200 cash payment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We see both the headline and core inflation rates slowing down for the past few months with core inflation down to 3.8% year-on-year in July compared to 4.2% in June.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While Cost-of-Living packages are rolled out to assist Singaporeans with inflation, businesses are facing immense challenges too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to inflation and rising cost, businesses in Singapore continue to have to contend with rising cost of production, tight labour market, challenges of attracting talent, managing workers expectations in the new norm, increasing global competition, MNEs re-shoring/near-shoring and governments around the world offering more grants, schemes and support to continue to attract investments into their country and giving us a run for our money.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we all want to pay our workforce better, this is only sustainable if it is done with a corresponding increase in productivity and through engaging in high value-added work and work in industries that are higher-valued to the world.
