speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Improving productivity, building capability, anchoring quality investments, nurturing and sustaining innovation is our lifeline to remain relevant in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thankfully, we are not short of tools to encourage companies to deliver what we need.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have the National Productivity Grant, with the additional $4 billion top up mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are investing $24 billion from 2021 to 2025 to catalyse research innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have specific industry transformation maps for 23 industries and many other schemes and policies that are aimed to drive productivity and nurture innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill proposes to enhance and have new tax deductions on qualifying expenditure through the new EIS to further nurture and sustain innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, businesses already enjoy tax deductions of up to 250% of qualifying expenditure on qualifying R&D activities, registration of IP, acquisition and licensing of IP rights and training expenditure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I am fully supportive of its intent, my clarification will focus more on the effectiveness of this tool and if we need to tweak it to meet the policy intent of encouraging businesses to engage in R&D, innovation and capability development activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To do so, my clarifications are broadly summarised in the following: firstly, how effective has the tax incentive been in developing new capability and R&D?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, can we expand the list of qualified partners for support on innovation projects?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Based on this, granted that it is a lot harder to quantify the benefits, does the Ministry have an estimate of how this has encouraged and enabled more innovation or generated more IPs in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It will be useful to have an idea if this is an effective lever to drive innovation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The tax deduction is applicable to "qualifying training expenditure incurred on courses that are eligible for SkillsFuture funding and aligned with the Skills Framework".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe the qualifying training expenditure on the courses eligible for EIS tax deduction is too broad, given that the policy objective is for EIS to encourage businesses to engage in R&D, innovation and develop deeper capability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To be fair, there are good and relevant courses in the SkillsFuture list, such as "Intellectual Property and Business Model Planning" and "Intellectual Property, Innovations in IoT".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Ministry consider narrowing down the number of courses so that businesses can sharpen their thinking when it comes to driving R&D, innovation and developing capability in their organisation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another consideration when assessing qualifying training expenditure in relation to delivering intended policy objectives is the assumption that skills learnt in training are applied and delivers a real value to the business.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can I also suggest that to qualify for tax deduction from the training expenditure, a business has to show that the trainee has delivered value to the organisation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, should we get the applying companies to briefly describe how their staff are applying the skillset to drive innovation and productivity in their organisation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I understand and appreciate that asking for proof of applying the learnt skillset may be challenging to administer, the smaller number of applications from a precise list of courses and the use of possibly AI and machine learning to assess the submissions could help in the administrative process.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will then ensure that businesses intending to claim this tax deduction will think through more thoroughly about how trainees can immediately put their newly acquired skillsets to further develop R&D and capability in the organisation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have mentioned about narrowing the number of eligible courses to focus more on productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have also touched on encouraging businesses to then apply the newly acquired skillset.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The next important element is then – who is eligible for the tax deduction for training expenditure in the company?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially important because since we now have the option to convert qualifying training expenditure into cash.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will make it harder for those who intend to abuse the system and send temporary "workers" for training indiscriminately and collect the training expenditure in cash.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On my last clarification, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill proposes that innovation projects carried out with polytechnics, ITEs and qualified partners may be eligible for tax deductions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will the Ministry review the list of partner institutions periodically?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Businesses are currently facing immense challenges from rising costs, a more competitive labour market, difficulties in attracting talent and increasing global competition.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While businesses wish to pay their workforce better, this is only sustainable if it is done with a corresponding increase in productivity, and through engaging in higher value-added work and work in industries which provide more value to the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Improving productivity, building capability, anchoring quality investments, nurturing and sustaining innovation is our lifeline to stay relevant in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This Bill proposes to enhance and contains new tax deductions on qualifying expenditure through the new EIS to further nurture and sustain innovation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I am fully supportive of its intent, my clarification will focus more on the effectiveness of this Bill to meet the policy intent of encouraging businesses to engage in R&D, innovation and capability development activities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The clarifications that I seek can be summarised as follows; firstly, how effective have tax incentives been in developing new capabilities and R&D; secondly, how do we ensure that investments in skills will give rise to productivity or effective capability development; and thirdly, can we expand the list of partners that qualify for support?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in conclusion, I believe the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill has changes that help align it better with policy objectives while improving tax administration.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The introduction of the EIS to encourage more businesses to engage in R&D, innovation and capability development is very much welcomed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications I have mentioned earlier, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I also note that this is your maiden speech in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments to this Bill are wide ranging.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Last week, I had the opportunity to participate in a study trip to Denmark.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Denmark ranks as one of the happiest countries.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Danish welfare state is characterised by an extensive social security system and high-income equality.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This has been possible with the Danish society willing to contribute high taxes in return for the system they now collectively enjoy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Their journey took time and is steeped in history.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It was not always easy and not without challenges.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The word "trust" was frequently used throughout our various interactions, whether this was learning about sustainability at Lego, whether it was about urban innovation and design at Bloxhub, rethinking issues requiring systemic change at the Danish Design Centre or teaching the entrepreneurial mindset, beginning all the way in primary school through to secondary school, at the Danish Foundation for Entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share three helpful lessons and observations from the many that I noted.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The first is that of a society that is not just surviving but thriving.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As I reflect on the many achievements in Singapore, we are thriving in several areas and surviving in others.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, we need to try to work toward a model where as many as possible not just survive with support packages but thrive in an environment that provides financial stability, high quality of life and the ability to make choices on what really matters.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Bloxhub in Copenhagen is a co-working community space that brings together architects, engineers, startups, policy-makers and academia to drive urban innovation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Creative thinking and collaboration begins at the very earliest stages.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Copenhagen, and I am using the figure that was given to us at the presentation, has a population of 600,000 – about a 10th of our population – and yet they have assembled an initiative to plan for a further increase for 100,000 – and this is an urban population – by 2050.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In their words, cities are systems, cities are nature, cities are communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Their continuing mission – to create liveable, resilient cities for the future – but they are planning well in advance.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The second observation is the practice of constant and continuing review of systems and processes across all sectors, whether these are social, health, green issues or digital transformation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Danish Design Center illustrated an example of their current study concerning youth mental health issues – and they start with the difficult questions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For example, is this an issue where youths are surviving in a sick system?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: They are now undergoing a comprehensive review of whether systemic change will be required to enable youths to thrive and not just survive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The third observation that we could consider is from the Danish Foundation for Entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The teaching of entrepreneurship has been found to help solve challenges creatively, help handle complex situations, look for available resources, network, increase motivation, amongst many, many other positives.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In the 10 years since implementation, the sample findings suggest entrepreneurship has been transformative.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One major objective is to keep Danish entrepreneurship at the forefront.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, as not everyone becomes an entrepreneur, their evaluation has shown that teaching entrepreneurship has developed a better workforce.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: IPCs across the spectrum of social services – medical and health services, education, culture, heritage, arts, sports – have had many years to build up a culture of giving, supported by this generous scheme.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The objective is to enable and encourage collaborative philanthropy in the non-profit sectors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some sectors, as we have heard, seem to have done better than others.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The matter of qualifying donations may benefit from a review, to enable access to funding by new initiatives that are charitable in nature, but have not yet achieved IPC status.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar way, smaller IPCs may be helped in ways to increase wider awareness of their mission.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This is being done through giving time, giving expertise and giving financially.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has laid one foundational piece for the coming years, further extending the 2.5 times deduction.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We should not delay demonstrating our collective responsibility to play our part.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The demands of an ageing society, the aspirations for better quality of life for those with specific needs and the vulnerable and the desire that no one gets left behind will need the active participation of both Government and people.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Planning and implementing may well take us beyond 2026.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For many years, we have been giving beyond our borders.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The interest and active initiatives include social entrepreneurs, foundations, religious organisations, educational institutions and volunteers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Thus far, all these initiatives have not received tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the continuing development of Singapore as a philanthropy hub and the proposed schemes for donations outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Public consultations have been a method to get feedback and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the feedback and suggestions are accepted.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Those that are not accepted get an explanation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Fifty-eight years ago, this nation with began with a group of dedicated leaders who transformed a small country with limited resources to the financial success that we enjoy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This has been a collaborative effort of leaders and people.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Today, we find ourselves as stewards of a success story and as Singaporeans, carry this responsibility for the current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The future will be different, in terms of challenges and aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are few ways we can think about taxes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the mechanism, it is the liver by which a government collects and redistributes resources to different segments of society, including the vulnerable and those who need it most.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a strategic level, tax policy is also an instrument that pools our collective resources to help us shape the society that we wish to see as a people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also the means by which we provide incentives for industries to move towards and sectors to grow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At its core, good tax policy can help foster the balance between social harmony and economic progress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are three broad areas I would like to discuss regarding the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will bring us in line with international standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, MOF has shared that it would not be practical to prescribe in legislation, minimum thresholds to establish economic substance, given the variety of business model and skill of operations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is the approach going to be on a case-by-case basis?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are some of the key principles that would distinguish businesses with economic substance and those without?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also understand that further guidance will be provided in an IRAS e-tax guide.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EIS is an investment to further secure Singapore's position as an Innovation Hub as it helps companies defray risks when undertaking R&D.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to the long incubation period for innovation and uncertainty, firms may think long and hard before committing upfront resources to innovation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Could the Senior Minister of State share more about the current restraints and constraints faced by companies undertaking capability development activities and how the EIS amendments aim to mitigate them and lower the barriers for smaller companies, in particular, which may be cash-strapped?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From a tax utility perspective, what are the factors are considered important by the Government for the R&D ecosystem to grow sustainably beyond subsidies?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any existing schemes or new ones which the Government is intending to create or to enhance domestic human capital capable of executing the R&D that the EIS hopes to support?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Alongside the broadening of the scope of eligible investments to include blended finance structures to recognise concessional capital, which aims to strengthen Singapore's position as a regional philanthropy hub.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also catalyse more investments into worthwhile social and climate projects.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to achieve this status, our philanthropic framework must tackle key issues of our time, which are typically global in nature and go beyond our shores.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, climate change and also at greater scale, for example, wider populations in Southeast Asia and not just Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our strategic trusted and neutral position in this region is prime for such operations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The growth in the number of family foundations, has generally followed the growth in family offices and I agree with the push towards encouraging family offices to anchor their giving operations in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While allowing tax deduction for overseas donations via qualifying local intermediaries shifts the longstanding principle of tax deductions for donations exclusively benefiting the Singapore community is an understandable step, I hope that we can put in further measures to proactively strengthen the nexus between family offices and our local charitable organisations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to ensure that firstly, overseas donations do not overshadow the proportion of domestic donations from these family offices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How long will it take for local intermediaries to qualify and what support is available to fund capacity building of social sector organisations?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would also be important to ensure that legislation such as fund regulations and charity laws remain clear and keep up with the times to enable the structuring of such new models.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, most will agree that our collective contributions should enable us to create a society which uplifts each and every citizen to thrive, regardless of where we start in life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Budget 2023, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong reaffirmed his commitment to this ideal.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in an inflationary environment with rising cost of living, many feel the pinch.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The execution of increasing taxes when it comes to real life and how we can and should go about raising funds to pay for increased support is often less straightforward.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In conversations, many often point to free healthcare and education systems in some other parts of the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But less spoken off, is the higher tax rates that come with it.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government debt or the culture which has been developed in these jurisdictions over time, leads to each individual seeing it as their responsibility to invest in their own society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This includes not just businesses, as corporate citizens, but everyday people too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To do so, we should do two things.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The changes are also to align our tax system with international tax developments and MOF's periodic reviews.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I wish to seek a few clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, smaller businesses, although potentially eligible for the EIS, might not have significant taxable income against which they can offset their investment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such cases, it is highly likely that most of these businesses would opt for the cash option.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, are there plans to review these figures, to ensure that they adequately cater to the needs of a broader spectrum of businesses?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, I could not resist drawing parallels between the EIS and the previous R&D incentives under the Productivity and Innovation Credit scheme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this connection, it begs the question of how effective the previous scheme had been, and whether these incremental changes will truly foster the desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The cost of research has also increased over the years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, the "$50,000 of qualifying innovation expenditure" may only make up for the small amount of research cost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this quantum be revised upwards to attract higher-end and more advanced research that may cost more but likewise attract more talent?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Government consider broadening the scope of the EIS to encompass joint ventures that closely collaborate with our local ecosystem and industries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By doing so, we can ensure that the benefits of this scheme extend beyond the immediate beneficiaries and contribute to the overall growth and development of the entire ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During the Budget deliberations, concerns were raised that the changes in the WMCR disincentivises higher-earning mothers to consider having more children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In certain cases, the policy changes would result in some individuals receiving fewer incentives than before.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Considering the feedback stemming from the policy change, I would like to inquire about the measures the Government has taken to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What steps have been taken to ensure that the changes in the WCMR scheme are effectively communicated to the public, along with the policy considerations that underlie this decision?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, are there plans in place to address any perceived disincentives amongst this group of working mothers, to ensure that they do not feel discouraged from expanding their families?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While it may be argued that the higher cash payouts may not be a factor for these group of mothers, a right signal needs to be sent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What specific policies and initiatives are being considered, and how will they be implemented to provide tangible support for this group?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, I have some queries on the proposed changes pertaining to mandating submission of income information by intermediaries for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What processes will be implemented to ensure that the intermediaries comply with this requirement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, what penalties will be imposed in the event of non-compliance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government plan to guarantee the accuracy of the information obtained through this mandate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given the diversity of occupations and income streams of SEPs, it is critical that we employ robust methods to validate this data, so as to prevent misuse or fraudulent claims.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does the Government intend to leverage advanced technologies, such as fraud detection algorithms or AI, to enhance accuracy and efficiency of this process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, will there be whistle-blowing policies in place?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recognising that there is no one-size-fits-all policy, it is imperative that we maintain a commitment to regularly review and adapt taxation policies to ensure their ongoing adequacy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, effective communication channels must be established to address public concerns and to make residents more aware of available alternatives and supporting policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments will encourage businesses to engage in R&D, and develop their capabilities through the EIS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through tax incentives, they will also encourage family offices in Singapore to base their philanthropic operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken up many times pushing to extend the WMCR to single unwed parents who are parents too and should not be discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the WMCR is to "encourage married women to remain in the workforce after having children".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is what is stated on the IRAS website, but it is not accurate as the relief is provided for divorcees too, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But again, why are single unwed parents left out?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be clear, single unwed parents can get the relief if they just marry the father of the child and then file for a divorce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But why make them jump through so many hoops to get something they should get in the first place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We want to encourage mothers to return to the workforce, but why not encourage single unwed mothers to return to the workforce too?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For single unwed mothers who do return to the workforce despite the absolutely difficult circumstances they are in, should we not support them and provide them with the WMCR?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This policy is not cast in stone and we are amending it now to provide more Government support for eligible lower- to middle-income working mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should provide support to single unwed mothers too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know the reply will be that we do provide support to single unwed parents and the Senior Minister of State might list the range of support provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that some support is there but this push for providing the WMCR is also about being fair and being inclusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is about making sure single unwed parents do not feel discriminated against.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single unwed parents have written to me, come to my Meet-the-People Session and speak to me during my home visits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hear them, I feel the stigma they face and the discrimination they endure daily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One single unwed parent wrote to me with regard to the WMCR and said, "Why the unfair treatment and discrimination for single mothers?" and "Many grievances ever since my baby was born and I am ashamed to be a Singapore citizen who is left out in the system." Let me stress that the appeal here, like the appeal to provide the single unwed parents with the cash component of the baby bonus and the parenthood tax rebate, is not about providing single unwed parents with more support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The appeal is that they be treated equally and be provided with the WMCR like how it is provided to married, divorced and widowed working mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on growing Singapore as a philanthropic hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I applaud the move to take an international perspective in growing Singapore's philanthropic work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this should not be limited to the top tiers of society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, can we look into how tax incentives can support individuals who wish to contribute to regional humanitarian causes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Helping to alleviate humanitarian crises contributes to regional stability, which in turn benefits Singapore as a country dependent on stable relations and predictable relations with her neighbours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Instead, the objective of this amendment is to address international tax avoidance risk by entities without real economic activities in Singapore, as well as that relating to foreign-sourced gains from the disposal of IP rights.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the latter, we will adopt the internationally-agreed modified nexus approach, which is also currently used for our Intellectual Property Development Incentive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we have designed this proposed change to be as targeted as possible, there should not be significant impact on genuine businesses with real activities here.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This move should be seen in the context of our broader policy to align key areas of our tax regime with international standards, such as the rules against harmful tax practices agreed by the Inclusive Framework on BEPS, as well as the EU COCG Guidance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As a small open economy, it is in our interest for our tax rules to stand up to international scrutiny, to facilitate the continued flow of trade and investments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Chandradas asked about the interaction between the proposed amendment and BEPS Pillar 2 rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the other hand, this proposed amendment aims to address tax avoidance risks associated with foreign-sourced disposal gains and is not confined to large MNEs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Chandradas and Ms Nadia also asked how IRAS would assess economic substance and operationalise the proposed change, while Mr Wee raised some scenarios relating to restructuring transactions, funds and family offices.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The answer is that the tax treatment will depend on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As business practices vary across industries, it would not be possible to prescribe quantitative tests.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Nevertheless, IRAS will certainly take sector-specific circumstances into account in administering the new rule.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MOF and IRAS have held several engagements with the industry over the last few months to hear businesses' feedback and understand their concerns, as IRAS works out the implementation details.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS will provide industry with guidance on how economic substance will be assessed to be adequate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Where possible, sector-specific circumstances and common scenarios, including those raised by Members of the House, will be considered and addressed in the guidance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS aims to publish the guidance by the end of this year and will refine it over time based on feedback and consultation with industry partners.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS will consider the suggestion from Ms Chandradas for an expedited advance ruling framework.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, foreign tax credit will be available based on current tax rules.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, the proposed amendment will not cover foreign entities that have no operations in Singapore other than the use of banking facilities here.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS will include these clarifications in their guidance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Overall, we do not expect the new tax treatment to have a negative impact on our economy, as our focus has always been on attracting and anchoring real economic activities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Our global competitiveness will not be affected, as these international standards are also applied in other jurisdictions, so there is a level-playing field.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat sought clarification on whether SEPs can opt out of having their income information submitted to IRAS by their intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms Jean See asked how such income information would be used and safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The use of such income information is governed and subject to existing safeguards under the Income Tax Act.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The information obtained would be used for tax administration purposes, including pre-filling of income tax returns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will make it more convenient for SEPs to submit their tax filings.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They will be able to verify and amend the pre-filled income amount before filing their tax returns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond tax, the income information collected will also help in the administration of social schemes, such as the WIS scheme, which I mentioned in my opening speech and Ms Mariam Jaafar spoke about this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Picture a 45-year-old SEP earning $1,500 a month.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He could have qualified for Workfare, but is not receiving it because he did not file his income tax returns and he did not make MediSave contributions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Tapping on intermediaries to submit income information on SEPs could also facilitate the administration of new schemes going forward, including financial assistance during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For instance, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the SEP Income Relief Scheme was rolled out to support SEPs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, as SEP income information was incomplete, the Government was only able to automatically disburse the payouts to some SEPs, and NTUC had to process applications from SEPs who did not automatically qualify.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Having the relevant data to quickly administer such support schemes will enable SEPs to receive the support more quickly, and also simplify administration of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Wee, Mr Saktiandi and Mr Parekh asked about the extension of this initiative to other intermediaries and whether the intermediaries would be provided with financial support to establish new infrastructure for regulatory reporting.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For intermediaries in other industries, such as ride hail service and taxi operators, food and goods delivery platform companies, IRAS will continue to engage them and work with them closely to understand and address potential operational and system issues, so as to keep the compliance burden low.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng enquired on how the Government will ensure that the intermediaries comply with the requirement and the accuracy of the information obtained as well as whether penalties will be imposed in the event of non-compliance and if there will be whistle-blowing policies in place.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To ensure compliance, IRAS will adopt an approach similar to that for the Auto-Inclusion Scheme for employers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: During the initial phase, IRAS will continue to render support to the intermediaries while adopting a light-touch approach such as issuing reminders or warning letters for non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS also has compliance programmes in place to detect and identify intermediaries who have made errors in the submission.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This includes assurance audits to ensure that intermediaries have adequate controls to maintain accurate information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: While intermediaries will not be unduly penalised for unintended errors or mistakes detected, they may be liable for offences if errors are due to negligence or without reasonable excuse.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS also has an existing whistle-blowing channel which the public can use to inform IRAS of any wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The FEDRs were developed using income and expense data for the different delivery modes, which IRAS obtained from its consultation with the industry and survey with the workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The current FEDRs strike a balance between simplifying tax compliance while ensuring that the ratios are reflective of the actual expense ratios of delivery workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For those whose actual expenses exceed the FEDRs, they can claim deductions based on the actual deductible expenses incurred.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms See and Ms Mariam asked whether IRAS intends to review the different FEDRs in the future to keep pace with changes in the costs of the delivery services and if the initiative on mandatory income submission by intermediaries could assist in this review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: IRAS will regularly review and assess the relevance of the FEDR rates based on available data, including income information obtained from intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, IRAS reviewed the existing 60% FEDR for private-hire car and taxi drivers, which was implemented in the YA2019; they did the review this year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The latest data showed that while drivers' expenses have increased, their revenue has also grown due to increases in meter and mileage rates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Therefore, the 60% FEDR remains relevant and sufficient for the majority of drivers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For those that this does not apply to because their expenses are higher, as I mentioned earlier, FEDR is optional; they can submit the actual expenses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip and Mr Saktiandi asked if the Government has taken measures to address these concerns and if we had considered alternatives in designing or redesigning the WMCR.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong had explained then, the WMCR change should not be seen in isolation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is part of a package of moves to support marriage and parenthood, which has been strengthened over the years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, we announced at Budget this year that we will be enhancing the Baby Bonus Scheme and parental leave provisions, which benefit all couples regardless of income.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Eligible working mothers of qualifying children born or adopted before 1 January 2024 will not be affected as they can continue to claim the WMCR based on the existing design.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As pointed out by Mr Sharael, the change in the WMCR reflects our social compact of a fairer society, one which we provide more support for the less well-off and, in this case, lower- and middle-income working mothers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to engage couples and parents to raise awareness of the package of support measures available for marriage and parenthood, including the enhancements announced during Budget 2023.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi also sought clarification on the rationale for removing Foreign Domestic Worker Levy Relief (FDWLR).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The FDWLR was introduced in 1989 to support working married women who needed the help of a domestic worker, so that they could return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Since then, the Government has introduced new schemes to directly support those caring for dependants, including working mothers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In particular, those living with children below 16 years old, elderly or persons with disabilities may enjoy a concessionary Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) levy of $60 per month instead of the usual levy of $300 or $450 per month for the first and subsequent FDW respectively.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We consider not just the year-to-year changes, or more importantly, the medium-term trend in our expenditures and revenues where we manage our fiscal resources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As we know, Singapore has an ageing population and we must expect that with an ageing population, there will be rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This has yet to account for additional spending that may arise from new policy initiatives, including the need to further invest in resilience and to strengthen our social compact and economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the revenue side, our tax revenue collections have grown broadly in line with GDP.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The higher tax revenue collection in FY2022 compared to the previous year is due to our economic recovery after the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is unclear whether the trend can continue, given the uncertain global macroeconomic outlook.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In the medium term, revenue generally does not grow faster than GDP without tax rate changes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why the revenue measures announced at the recent Budgets, including the GST increase this year and next year, remain necessary to meet our medium-term spending needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Deferring the GST increase will only store up more problems for the future, leaving us with less resources to take care of our growing fiscal needs and we cannot count on short-term upsides to fund structural needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When the Government has unexpected fiscal upsides, we share these surpluses with Singaporeans, including providing relief for households through Cost-of-Living Support Packages.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael mentioned this in his speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I will just name two components, for information.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And we will also increase the special payments that eligible Singaporeans will receive, and there will be 2.5 million eligible Singaporeans by the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there will be an amount, depending on your income, but up to $800 per eligible Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this will include many of our Singaporeans, including our retirees who are staying in private properties because this does not look at your property type.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It looks at your income, as long as you do not own two or more properties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we understand that Singaporeans are concerned about the GST increase and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On delaying the GST increase for one or two years, what we have done is actually better than that.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: With the Assurance Package, we have delayed the impact of GST increase for the majority of Singaporean households by five years and by about 10 years for lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government remains committed to doing so even with elevated inflation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is why we have substantially enhanced the Assurance Package over the past two years, and the Government has also announced additional support measures to help families with rising costs of living beyond the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is some additional relief for all Singaporeans, with more for lower- and middle-income groups.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is less expansionary than the previous years' Budget and this is to avoid adding to elevated inflationary pressures while supporting our economy and helping families in a more uncertain global environment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We achieve this balanced outcome by focusing more of our support measures on the lower- and middle-income groups while providing some help for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Allow me to share more about the scheme, and in doing so, address their questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: First, under the PTIS, approved qualifying donors can claim 100% tax deductions for overseas donations made through qualifying local intermediaries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Overseas donations refer to cash donations made towards any charitable, benevolent or philanthropic purpose whose main objective is to benefit persons, events or objects outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These could include overseas philanthropic causes in sustainability that Mr Wee mentioned, as long as all the other criteria are met.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MAS is committed to processing applications to be approved qualifying donors and local intermediaries in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Second, to ensure oversight as highlighted by Ms Mariam, MAS requires all participating SFOs, to submit annual review returns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, as SFOs are required to channel their donations through local qualifying intermediaries, these intermediaries also conduct due diligence checks.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Third, to benefit from the PTIS, SFOs would have to meet two conditions: first, appoint and maintain a Philanthropy Professional at the point of application and throughout the incentive approval period; and second, incur an additional $200,000 in Local Business Spending and employ an additional local professional headcount in the financial year when the overseas donations are made.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These conditions that Ms Chandradas asked about are made known upfront to the SFO applicants and they are required to declare that they have met the conditions in their annual returns to MAS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If the conditions are not met, the legislation provides for the Government to claw back the previously granted tax deductions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Fourth, Members spoke about ensuring that the local charity sector is not excluded from the benefits of PTIS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Qualifying local intermediaries would include IPCs with a valid permit for "Fundraising for Foreign Charitable Purposes".

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Overall, some Members advocated for more overseas philanthropic giving across a wider spectrum of society, while others spoke about the need to ensure that the philanthropic giving also supports local causes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I am glad that Members agree that philanthropy makes our society better and, given their different views between overseas and local giving, that they appreciate that the Government needs to strike a balance between the two.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond the PTIS, the Government has other tax incentive schemes to encourage local philanthropy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will continue to review our schemes to foster and sustain the spirit of giving.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi asked about the rationale behind raising R&D tax deductions to 400%.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The parameters of the EIS are set to provide modest but meaningful support for businesses in their drive to invest in R&D.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Looking across comparable economies which offer similar tax deductions on R&D activities, a 400% tax deduction is competitive when compared to jurisdictions, such as Hong Kong and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Sharael and Ms Nadia asked about the effectiveness of tax deductions on innovation and its outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: R&D tax measures do lead to an increase in innovation activities as they help to mitigate risks and give an additional boost to returns on investments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That said, tax deductions cannot operate in isolation and must also be complemented by a developed R&D ecosystem to promote innovation, which the Government continues to invest in through our Research, Innovation and Enterprise plans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: During the same period, we also saw almost a three-fold increase in sales revenue from commercialised products attributed to R&D performed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are promising trends, but we know there is room for our economy and enterprises to invest even more in R&D so that we can be more globally competitive.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The EIS, together with our broader ecosystem of grants, incentives, financing tools and R&D talent, will give businesses an additional boost.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip, Mr Wee and Mr Huang highlighted the importance of encouraging our local SMEs to take advantage of the EIS to innovate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The tax deduction will apply for qualifying innovation projects carried out with partner institutions such as the polytechnics, ITE and the Centres of Innovation, and could relate to business process redesign or deployment of productivity equipment.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These would not be considered "R&D" in the strictest sense, but are nonetheless useful to help SMEs to kickstart their innovation journey.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Undertaking innovation projects with these partner institutions will also enable SMEs to tap on the existing expertise there instead of having to acquire or develop their own.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Yip asked if the expenditure cap of $50,000 can be revised upwards to cover higher-end research with higher costs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Businesses that undertake research that meets the R&D definition can tap on the enhanced deductions for their higher R&D costs, which has a higher expenditure cap of $400,000.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Many of the projects undertaken in partnership with the universities would be able to qualify for the enhanced R&D or IP-related deductions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Nonetheless, we will observe the uptake of this new deduction for innovation and consider whether we could expand the list of partner institutions where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I also thank Ms See for highlighting the cashflow concerns of businesses when they undertake innovation activities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will monitor and study how we can further support our businesses in their innovation journey, including encouraging them to work with NTUC to form company training committees.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ms See suggested providing some upfront subsidy for innovation, similar to what we are doing for training courses.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the context between innovation and training is quite different.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Unlike training courses, which can be pre-approved and subsidised upfront, investments in innovation are varied, differing by sector, scope and the businesses' level of maturity.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is therefore difficult to pre-approve innovation expenditures or provide upfront subsidy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Beyond Government support schemes like EIS, it is important for businesses to take the initiative and embark on the innovation journey to improve their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They have to set aside adequate cashflow for investing in new equipment and developing the necessary capabilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Wee and Ms Nadia asked about the development of human capital to support businesses' innovation activities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael also asked if the list of eligible courses should be narrowed down.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These courses support industry transformation and workforce development needs and will support a range of enterprises from different industries at various stages of their innovation journey.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They also include courses that cater to freelancers from the creative industries.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SkillsFuture Singapore will continue to monitor the relevance and effectiveness of courses eligible for EIS deductions and refine the list of courses accordingly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Sharael asked if the Government could request proof of value before the tax deduction on training is granted and if the deduction can be limited to employees who have served a minimum number of years to minimise abuse of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This will help to ensure that the firm sends its employees for training only if it will create value for the firm and support its innovation efforts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The firm, the employer has skin in the game.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Ultimately, what we want is to have a scheme that can support companies to embark on innovation because we know innovation is key to future economic growth, it is key to creating good jobs for our workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I encourage businesses to learn more about the EIS through the information available on the IRAS website and we will also work with industry partners such as our trade associations and chambers to raise awareness among businesses.

text: Any clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?
